boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Haslach (= Albeck) entry (11 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Dupont's 1st division of Ney's 6th corps, with Sahuc's dragoon brigade and the 1st hussars, against the Austrian army at Ulm, Bodart naming FML Prince Schwarzenberg. The dragoons on foot's march, the Austrian cavalry's raid on the parks at Albeck and the night withdrawal to Albeck are within the boundary only as they bear on the action; Elchingen (B364b, 14 October) and the 1806 inquiry into Baraguey d'Hilliers' conduct are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Austrian) 25,000 men under FML Prince Schwarzenberg and side A (French) 6,000 men under General of Division Dupont. By his stated rule these are the forces available for the engagement, not only those that fought, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several (scoping decision 1). He does not say which formations he counted or at what moment. His 6,000 for side A is close to Alombert and Colin's 6,400 with patrols and detachments (claim alombert-composition) and to the returns' 6,194 infantry and cavalry (our sum; claim side-a-return). His 25,000 for side B is the figure Dupont gave for the Austrians he fought (claim french-figures-for-side-b) and lies above Krauss's estimate of the Austrians engaged (claim krauss-side-b-engaged); Krauss gives no total for the army at Ulm (claim krauss-side-b-army). The passages read do not say which figures Bodart used. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'.

claims.value: Side A's returns at the crossing of the Rhine, in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV (late September 1805), list the 6th corps' 1st division as the 9e légère (2 battalions, 1,763 men), the 32e de ligne (2 battalions, 1,662) and the 96e (2 battalions, 1,721): 6 battalions and 5,146 men by our sum. The corps' 1st hussars had 3 squadrons, 375 men and 408 troop horses. In the cavalry reserve's return the 4th dragoon division's 15th dragoons had 3 squadrons, 322 men and 317 horses, and its 17th 3 squadrons, 351 men and 352 horses. Both returns' totals are headed 'présents sous les armes' (present under arms). Ney's order for the action gives the 1st division as under General Dupont; Krauss says a dragoon brigade of two regiments was attached to Dupont's division at Albeck, and Dupont's journal names it as Sahuc's, of the 15th and 17th, joined the evening before the action.
claims.rationale: Side A's own figures for the troops at Haslach, read from the page images. They are some two weeks older than the action and show neither the losses of the march nor detachments: Ney left Dupont two squadrons of the 1st hussars, not three (claim side-a-orders), and half of Dupont's cavalry was out on reconnaissance (claim alombert-composition). The returns print no division subtotal, so 5,146 is our sum, the total Alombert and Colin also print; 6,194 is our sum of the division, the hussars and the two dragoon regiments. The corps' artillery is listed separately and is not added. The date conversion uses the editors' own equation of 19 vendémiaire with 11 October 1805. The force was attached before the action by Ney's orders, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): '6th army corps at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; 'cavalry reserve at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; 'total of those present under arms'; 'under the orders of General Dupont, will blockade Ulm on the left bank of the Danube'; Krauss, 'in the 6th corps (Ney) a dragoon brigade (two regiments) was attached to Dupont's division standing at Albeck'; 'the brigade of dragoons, commanded by General Sahuc, made up of the 15th and 17th regiments, which had joined the division the evening before'; 'day of 19 vendémiaire (11 October)'.

claims.value: Alombert and Colin give side A at Haslach as the 9e léger (1,763 present), the 32e de ligne (1,662 present) and the 96e de ligne (1,721 present), six battalions or 5,146 infantry; the 15th and 17th dragoons (673 horses) and the 1st hussars (375 horses), 'of which half was dispersed in reconnaissance', made up its cavalry; there may have been 250 gunners and train soldiers to serve the division's eleven pieces (two 12-pounders, six 8-pounders, two 4-pounders and a howitzer) and the three howitzers attached to the light cavalry. In all, patrols and detachments included, there were 6,400 men and fourteen pieces. A 4-pounder was under repair on 11 October, and their narrative has thirteen pieces in action.
claims.rationale: The French official history's figures, read from the page image. The infantry figures are the return's (claim side-a-return). The '673 horses' and '375 horses' equal the returns' men (322 + 351 = 673, our sum; 375), not their horses (669, our sum; 408), and Sahuc's report counts his brigade's casualties 'out of 673' (claim side-a-losses-reported). The listed parts sum to 6,444 (our sum) against the printed 6,400. Which units the 'half' refers to is not clear from the sentence; elsewhere they say the 1st hussars had no more than 150 to 200 men engaged, the rest being on reconnaissance (claim side-a-engaged). The force was the division with the cavalry Ney left it (claim side-a-orders), present before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'for his part he had the 9th light (1,763 present), the 32nd of the line (1,662 present) and the 96th of the line (1,721 present), that is six battalions or 5,146 men of infantry; the 15th and 17th dragoons (673 horses) and the 1st hussars (375 horses), of which half was dispersed in reconnaissance, made up his cavalry; there may have been 250 gunners and soldiers of the train to serve the eleven pieces of Dupont's division (two 12-pounders, six 8-pounders, two 4-pounders and a howitzer) and the three howitzers attached to the light cavalry (1). In all, patrols and detachments included, there were 6,400 men and fourteen pieces there'; 'the three howitzers remaining with the army corps accompany the light cavalry; a 4-pounder is under repair on 11 October'; 'our thirteen pieces hold their own against a superior artillery'.

claims.value: Side A's figures for its troops engaged: Dupont's division journal says 5,000 French came to fight 25,000 Austrians, the two other divisions not attacking on the right bank, and his report as the 6th corps journal gives it that 5,100 men fought for five hours against an army of 25,000. By the journal the 9th and 96th alone disputed the ground between Haslach and Jungingen for three hours, while a battalion of the 32nd and the two squadrons of the 1st hussars made up the whole left wing; Alombert and Colin say the 1st hussars had no more than 150 to 200 men engaged, the rest being on reconnaissance.
claims.rationale: Engaged forces as side A's sources give them, read from the page images; the boundary is unresolved and the figures, which describe different parts of the field, are not added. The 5,000 and 5,100 are Dupont's own statements, made by the commander whose conduct they describe, and Krauss disputes when Dupont first gave his figures (claim french-figures-for-side-b). English renderings (ours): '5,000 French come to fight 25,000 Austrians, the two other divisions not attacking on the right bank (1)'; '5,100 men fought for five hours against an army of 25,000 men and beat it completely'; 'then the 9th and 96th regiments must redouble their efforts and activity'; 'it is with these two regiments alone that we had for three hours to dispute the ground that separates Haslach from Jungingen'; 'the battalion of the 32nd and the two squadrons of the 1st hussars, which made up our whole left wing, were overwhelmed by numbers (2)'; '(2) the Austrians take 69 prisoners from the 1st hussars, which had no more than 150 to 200 men engaged, the rest being on reconnaissance, etc.'.

claims.value: Krauss says side B's whole army in Germany, except Kienmayer's corps, which continued its retreat to Munich on 10 October, and the small Wolfskeel detachment, was united at Ulm on 10 October; it had arrived early that day after the night retreat in a completely shattered state and had taken position with the greater part on the north bank of the Danube. By the morning report of 11 October the three-battalion infantry regiment Jellachich counted only 800 men instead of 2,800, of whom only 596 firearms; the regiment Kaunitz, with staff and four fusilier battalions, only 1,932 men instead of 3,700, of whom 1,693 firearms; and the grenadier battalion Jellachich only 4 officers and 108 men instead of 620, of whom 91 muskets.
claims.rationale: Side B's available force as Krauss gives it, read from the page image; the passages read give no total for the army at Ulm, which is not the force engaged (claim krauss-side-b-engaged). Alombert and Colin, citing an eyewitness, name Kaunitz among the first battalions engaged (claim side-b-units), but no passage says how many of its battalions fought. The army was at Ulm before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'the Austrian army had arrived at Ulm early on the 10th, as already mentioned, after the night retreat in a completely shattered state and had taken up a position with the greater part on the northern bank of the Danube'; 'with the exception of Kienmayer's corps, which continued its retreat on 10 October as far as Munich, and with the exception of the small detachment of Wolfskeel, the whole German army was thus united at Ulm on 10 October'; 'thus the infantry regiment Jellachich, three battalions strong, counted by the morning report of 11 October only 800 men instead of 2800, among them only 596 firearms, that is 199 firearms per battalion. The regiment Kaunitz, with staff and four fusilier battalions, counted only 1932 men instead of 3700, among them 1693 firearms, that is 424 muskets per battalion. The grenadier battalion Jellachich counted instead of 620 men only 4 officers and 108 men, among them 91 muskets'.

claims.value: Units of side B named in the action: Alombert and Colin, citing Schönhals, have General Loudon, attacked at Jungingen, retake the village first with some battalions and then with the regiment Froon as reinforcement; citing an eyewitness, they name the first Austrian battalions engaged as A. Louis, A. Reynier and Kaunitz; and they identify the cavalry that reached the French rear as two cuirassier regiments (Mack and Archduke Albert) and the La Tour light horse. Sahuc's report, as they quote it, names the Rosenberg light horse. Krauss names battalions of the regiment Riese sent to support the outposts and the regiment Rosenberg as the first cavalry to attack, and says FML Gottesheim's regiments were spread over different points of the position, Rainer and Manfredini fighting out of his sight.
claims.rationale: Unit names without strengths; neither history gives an order of battle for the action in the passages read, and the two name different units. The Kaunitz figures of the morning of 11 October (claim krauss-side-b-army) do not say how many of its battalions fought. Gottesheim's relation is known only through Krauss; its date is in the OCR and is not restated. English renderings (ours): '(1) journal of Dupont's division. According to the best Austrian relation that we have (Schönhals, Der Krieg 1805, Vienna 1873), General Loudon, attacked at Jungingen, retook this village a first time with some battalions, then a second time with the regiment Froon as reinforcement, and remained its master for good'; 'the first Austrian battalions engaged (A. Louis, A. Reynier and Kaunitz) fought rather slackly, by the account of an eyewitness (de Launay, staff captain in the Austrian service. A. G.)'; '(1) they were two regiments of cuirassiers (Mack and Archduke Albert) and the La Tour light horse'; 'at that moment the Rosenberg light horse moved off to charge a battalion of the 96th infantry regiment'; Krauss, 'the Austrians had sent some battalions of the regiment Riese forward to support the outposts'; 'first the regiment Rosenberg attacked the French infantry'; 'FML Gottesheim mentions in his relation of the action of Haslach, written on ... October, that his regiments "were distributed over different points of the position". The regiments Rainer and Manfredini fought outside his field of view'.

claims.value: Side A's figures for side B: the 6th corps journal for 11 October says that when the 1st division reached Haslach the enemy deployed in high works on the Spitzberg considerable forces estimated at 20,000 to 25,000 men; Dupont's division journal says 5,000 French came to fight 25,000 Austrians; and Alombert and Colin say that the same evening Dupont wrote to Ney that 5,100 men had fought for five hours against an army of 25,000 and beaten it completely. Krauss says Dupont spoke only of a victory over more than 25,000 Austrians, that the first surviving document in which Dupont claims to have beaten 25,000 Austrians is dated 13 October, the day he sent his combat report to Ney, and that Ney's report to Berthier of 12 October, sent on Dupont's first news, gives no Austrian strength; on 10 October Dupont had reported only that his reconnaissance detachment had met superior forces and that considerable enemy troops were gathered at Ulm.
claims.rationale: Side A's statements about side B, kept separate; all figures are read from page images. When Dupont first gave the 25,000 is disputed between the two histories (open questions): Alombert and Colin date it to the evening of the action, and print the passage in the 6th corps journal for 19 vendémiaire (11 October), while Krauss's two notes refer to the Sanson letter and to Dupont's report 'sent on the 21st' (21 vendémiaire, 13 October by the editors' equation of 19 vendémiaire with 11 October). The corps journal and Dupont's figures come from the same side and, for the 25,000, from Dupont himself, so they are not independent. English renderings (ours): '1st division: the division moves forward to surround Ulm; it had hardly arrived at Haslach when the enemy brought the artillery of his entrenchments into play against the division and deployed in high works on the Spitzberg hill considerable forces estimated at 20,000 to 25,000 men'; '5,000 French come to fight 25,000 Austrians'; 'that same evening, seeing his adversary withdraw on Ulm, he wrote to Ney:'; '5,100 men fought for five hours against an army of 25,000 men and beat it completely'; Krauss, 'Dupont spoke in his report and in other letters only of the victory that his division, which held the field of battle, won over more than 25,000 Austrians'; 'about the strength of the Austrians at Ulm Dupont sent two reports on 10 October. In the first report he stated that the reconnaissance detachment had come upon superior forces, in the second report that considerable enemy troops were united at Ulm (p. 364)'; 'the first surviving document in which Dupont claims to have beaten 25,000 Austrians is dated 13 October. He mentions nothing in it of the "whole Austrian army". On the same day he sent his combat report to Ney, in which he states that captured officers testified that the whole army had camped on the Michelsberg'; 'Ney's report to Berthier of 12 October, which had gone off on the first news from Dupont, contains no figures for the strength of the Austrians at Ulm, which can only be explained by Dupont having mentioned nothing in his report to Ney about the strength of the forces that had stood against him'; '1) Dupont's letter to General Sanson. Alombert et Colin, III, p. 523'; '2) Alombert et Colin, III, p. 511, note 1'; '(1) the report sent on the 21st by Dupont to Marshal Ney is identical with the fragment of journal that we have reproduced'.

claims.value: The Emperor, going to Munich, put Ney under Murat but had him first take Ulm, writing to him directly: 'surround Ulm in the course of tomorrow'; the dragoons on foot stayed under Ney's orders. Ney left Dupont two squadrons of the 1st hussars and two dragoon regiments of Bourcier's division, and sent his orders for the 11th late on the evening of the 10th: the 1st division under General Dupont was to blockade Ulm on the left bank of the Danube. On the morning of the 11th a third instruction told him to get ladders and tackle to scale Ulm's walls. Dupont replied that he was marching at once on Ulm.

claims.value: Dupont's decisions on the field: at Haslach he chose to fight rather than retreat (Alombert and Colin: 'Dupont accepted battle'; his later letter: 'I decided for the latter course'). General Rouyer had placed the 9th light on the Ulm road in front of Haslach; General Marchand deployed the 32nd on the left and put the 96th in reserve, the 1st hussars covering the left; Colonel Darricau held Haslach with a battalion of the 32nd, and Marchand posted its other battalion at the point of the wood on the right. As the enemy gained on the French right, Dupont put the 96th in line on the 9th's right, told Colonel Meunier of the 9th that he meant to charge the advancing line, and ordered General Sahuc to charge the enemy cavalry. Krauss says Dupont brought his reserve up beside the 9th light and decided to forestall the Austrian attack, and that after holding at Haslach until dark he withdrew his exhausted troops to Albeck.
claims.rationale: Decisions as Dupont's division journal, his later letter, the French official history and Krauss give them. Alombert and Colin give Dupont's reason as not wanting to encourage the enemy to take the offensive or to reveal that the Nördlingen road was open; Krauss leaves open whether the order to avoid superior forces (claim side-a-orders) was simply hard to follow or Dupont disobeyed it deliberately. English renderings (ours): 'to withdraw would have been to encourage the enemy to take the offensive, to reveal to him that the road to Nördlingen was open'; 'Dupont accepted battle'; 'it was necessary to choose without deliberating between retreat and battle: I decided for the latter course'; 'General Rouyer had placed the 9th light infantry on the Ulm road in front of Haslach; General Marchand at once has the 32nd deploy on the left and places the 96th in reserve. The 1st hussar regiment covered the left'; 'Colonel Darrieau with a battalion of the 32nd held the position of Haslach'; 'the second battalion of the 32nd, commanded by M. Bouge, had been carried by General Marchand to the point of the wood which was on our right'; 'the enemy's progress on our right flank obliges the general to put the 96th regiment into line at once: it takes its place on the right of the 9th'; 'General Dupont informs Colonel Meunier, commanding the 9th regiment, that his intention is to charge that line, which was gaining ground'; 'General Dupont gave General Sahuc the order to charge the enemy cavalry, which far outflanked his right'; Krauss, 'Dupont, who brought the reserve forward on the right beside the 9th light regiment, decided to forestall this attack'; 'until nightfall Dupont held at Haslach, but then he withdrew his exhausted troops, who had suffered heavily, to Albeck'; 'the action at Haslach now gives proof either that such an order is hard to follow'; 'that Dupont was disobedient deliberately and in full awareness'.

claims.value: No other side A troops joined the action. Ney's orders for the 11th to Dupont and to Baraguey d'Hilliers, whose dragoons on foot were to support Dupont, went by one staff officer, who lost his way at night in the flooded marshes and delivered Dupont's order first and Baraguey d'Hilliers' afterwards. Baraguey d'Hilliers, not thinking special haste was called for, sent his departure order only after midday and chose to wait for the men he had detached on Ney's order; his columns reached Albeck and Langenau only after dark, and the 6th corps journal has his division bivouac at Langenau to support the 1st division. He rode ahead to Albeck, arriving at about 4 o'clock by Alombert and Colin, but with his columns far behind could bring no help to the troops fighting; Dupont's letter announcing his march was the only one he received from Dupont that day. The corps' other divisions, on the right bank, did not attack. Krauss says Murat's and Lannes's dispositions ruled out their support; that Murat, in his report of the 12th, said Ney had ordered Dupont not to attack and to stay at Albeck, an order no one else mentions; that the discord between Murat and Ney may have caused disorder in the issue of orders; and that Dupont received Ney's order to cross to the right bank at Albeck in the evening.
claims.rationale: Why Dupont fought alone, as the French official history and Krauss give it. They divide the responsibility between Ney's staff, which Alombert and Colin blame for sending one officer on a double errand through the marshes at night, Baraguey d'Hilliers and the marshals, so the phase is unresolved. The times of the orders' delivery are disputed ('as always the times do not agree', Krauss), and the hours given in the OCR are not restated. The 1806 inquiry into Baraguey d'Hilliers' conduct, whose papers Alombert and Colin print, was not read. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'Ney's orders to Dupont and to Baraguay d'Hilliers were to be carried in the night to 11 October by a general staff officer from Günzburg to Albeck and Stotzingen'; 'but he lost his way in the night so badly in the water-covered moors'; 'this officer lost his way, took to the left and, after wandering in the marshes,'; 'that it was better first to hand General Dupont the order that concerned him'; 'the order was then handed to General Baraguey d'Hilliers, who, not believing he need bring any very special haste to its execution, sent off his order of departure only after midday'; 'thought it better to wait for the 1500 to 2,000 men that he had detached at Brenz, Lonthal, etc., on the Marshal's order'; 'the columns reached Albeck and Langenau only after nightfall'; 'as always the times do not agree'; 'it was a very culpable levity to send a single officer to carry out a double mission'; 'dragoons on foot: this division, leaving Stötzingen, went to Langenau, where it remained in bivouac to support the 1st division'; Krauss, 'the dragoons on foot could therefore not support Dupont's division in the fight at Haslach, which was over toward ... in the evening'; 'the testimony of General Baraguey d'Hilliers confirms the previous one; this general, going ahead of his division, arrived at Albeck at about 4 o'clock with a weak escort:'; Krauss, 'since his columns were still far behind, he could bring no help to the troops fighting in front'; Dupont to Baraguey d'Hilliers, 'the division I command is marching on Ulm. Arrived at Haslach, I will let you know my position'; Baraguey d'Hilliers' note, 'it is the only one I received from General Dupont on the day of the 19th'; 'the two other divisions not attacking on the right bank'; Krauss, 'a support of these troops by Murat and Lannes was ruled out by the dispositions of these two marshals'; 'is made very probable by the wording of Murat's report of the 12th to the Emperor, in which he tries to explain Dupont's isolated attack on Ulm'; Murat, 'he stayed on the 11th at Günzburg and Leipheim and sent Dupont the order to refrain from the attack and keep his position at Albeck; but that general was already in action with the enemy when he received this order'; 'this order, not to attack and to stay at Albeck, nobody else mentions, neither Ney nor Dupont'; 'at this time there were strong discords between Murat and Ney'; 'this relation between the two leaders may also have been the cause of some disorder in the issue of orders'; 'on the other hand Dupont received in the presence of the commander of the 1st brigade of the dragoons on foot, after ... in the evening at Albeck, the order of Ney quoted above to march to the right bank of the Danube'.

claims.value: Krauss says that at the generals' conference on the evening of 10 October the Archduke told Mack he had just received the Emperor's note instructing him to follow Mack's advice at all times, which in effect put the army commander under Mack's command; from then on Mack acted wholly on his own, issuing all orders directly and as a rule telling the named army commander only afterwards or not at all. On the morning of the 11th Mack told Colonel Bianchi he alone had the Emperor's authority to command the army and the Archduke should not imagine himself to be the commanding general. Because all formations had been broken up, no general knew where he was to command, and Krauss judges that higher command almost wholly failed during the action, the army's leader preferring to charge at the head of his regiment. Archduke Ferdinand's report of 12 October says the turning of the right wing was actually ordered by Prince Schwarzenberg and carried out by him and FML Klenau, Mack being present.
claims.rationale: Command relations from an Austrian history based on the Kriegsarchiv files, quoting Bianchi's diary and the Archduke's report; the relation of command was set by the Emperor's letter before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. Who directed side B at Haslach is not settled: Bodart names Schwarzenberg, the Archduke credits Schwarzenberg with the decisive move and Mack's relation credits Mack (claim side-b-decisions). English renderings (ours): 'in the evening a conference of all the army's generals took place, at which Mack announced his plan to march off with the army by Heidenheim'; 'on this occasion the Archduke told FML Mack that he had just received a note from the Emperor of ... October'; 'after the conference on the evening of 10 October'; 'this note instructed the Archduke to follow FML Mack's advice at all times, that is, it in fact placed the army commander under the command of FML Mack'; 'from now on acted wholly independently; he issued all orders directly and as a rule brought them to the knowledge of the appointed army commander only afterwards or not at all'; 'when Colonel Bianchi came to Mack with FML Gyulai early on 11 October'; 'he had received from the Emperor the sole authority to command the army; he alone was responsible for every proceeding'; 'His Royal Highness should not imagine himself to be the commanding general'; 'because all formations had been torn apart, no general knew where he was actually to command'; 'so during the action the higher command seems to have failed almost entirely, all the more as the army leader too preferred to ride a charge at the head of his regiment instead of exercising the supreme command in the action'; the Archduke, 'only I must remark here that the number of the dead, prisoners and captured guns is exaggerated, and that the turning of the right wing was actually ordered by Prince Schwarzenberg and carried out by him and FML Klenau. FML Mack was present, however'; '(Mack charged with them at the head of his regiment.'.

claims.value: Side B's decisions in the action, as the sources give them: the Austrians sent some battalions of the regiment Riese forward to support their outposts and, when these were thrown back, threw all the battalions of their right wing and several squadrons against the French attack. After the fight on the southern wing had begun, troops were sent forward via Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right, and fresh forces kept being brought up. The Archduke's report says the turning of the right wing was ordered by Prince Schwarzenberg and carried out by him and FML Klenau; Mack's relation says Mack had a considerable part of the left wing advance and led it into the rear of the enemy right. By Schönhals, as Alombert and Colin cite him, General Loudon retook Jungingen twice. Austrian cavalry pursued the French hussars and dragoons as far as Albeck. Dupont's journal says the enemy's movement was decided on the spot.
claims.rationale: Decisions as Krauss, the Archduke's and Mack's reports he quotes, Schönhals through Alombert and Colin, and Dupont's journal give them. Who ordered the envelopment is disputed between the Archduke's report and Mack's relation; Krauss's narrative gives the moves without naming who ordered them, and judges that higher command almost wholly failed (claim side-b-command). The moves were decided on the field, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'the Austrians had sent some battalions of the regiment Riese forward to support the outposts'; 'against this attack all the battalions of the Austrian right wing and several squadrons were thrown one after another'; 'at the time when the fight on the southern wing had already begun, Austrian troops were directed forward over Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right wing'; 'the Austrians, however, kept bringing up new forces'; the Archduke, 'the turning of the right wing was actually ordered by Prince Schwarzenberg and carried out by him and FML Klenau. claims.value: Both histories read qualify the result. Krauss says both sides claimed the victory, that in reality Dupont suffered a sensible tactical defeat, shown by the loss of 9 guns, 31 ammunition vehicles and 2 eagles, and that the action was no French victory, though Dupont could claim the victory with some show of right, having taken rich trophies and evacuated Haslach of his own accord only after dark, when the fighting had died down. Alombert and Colin call Dupont's 'complete success' excessively optimistic: the French had not been driven back behind their starting point, but Jungingen remained the enemy's, and on the left there was no illusion possible; the enemy could consider himself victorious while Dupont still held in front of Jungingen, but did not use his forces to make his success decisive.
claims.rationale: The histories' judgments of the result; neither reverses Bodart's winner, and Krauss's figures are read from the page image. English renderings (ours): 'both parties claimed the victory'; 'in reality Dupont, as could not be otherwise, suffered a sensible tactical defeat, to which the loss of 9 guns, 31 ammunition vehicles and 2 eagles bears clear witness'; 'although the action of Haslach was no victory of the French'; 'nevertheless Dupont could lay claim to the victory with a show of right: he had taken rich trophies and had evacuated Haslach voluntarily only after nightfall and after the fighting had died away'; '"the success was complete," he says again, "night came and we remained masters of the battlefield". That was excessively optimistic. To tell the truth, we had not been driven back behind our starting point, but Jungingen remained the enemy's'; 'there was no illusion possible on our left'; 'and although the enemy could consider himself victorious, Dupont still held in front of Jungingen'; 'but he did not know how to use the forces at his disposal to make his success decisive'.

claims.value: Bodart describes Haslach as a village in Württemberg 10 km northeast of Ulm. The French formed in front of Haslach, which served as the pivot of their movements, and fought over the plain and the ground between Haslach and the village of Jungingen; the Austrian line deployed on the heights of Jungingen and advanced into the plain. There were small woods on the French front, a wood at whose point the French right was posted, a small wood northeast of Jungingen with an Austrian battery, the woods north of Haslach into which the dragoons were driven, and a sunken road. The Austrian forces stood between Böfingen and Örlingen and, in side A's accounts, in high works on the Spitzberg. Snow and rain over several days had made the ground extremely difficult; the artillery report calls it broken, and on the retreat the guns overturned crossing ditches. Krauss notes that the lasting rain had flooded the Danube lowlands far and wide.

claims.value: Krauss says Dupont's division set out from Albeck toward Ulm at 11 a.m. on 11 October. Baraguey d'Hilliers, acknowledging Ney's orders, wrote that his dragoons on foot were somewhat dispersed and had marched or bivouacked all night in frightful weather, the roads were broken up and the artillery would have great difficulty arriving. Of Dupont's guns a 4-pounder was under repair; at Haslach the French artillery, much inferior to the enemy's, was partly dismounted and several pieces had their horses killed, the snow and rain of several days having made the ground extremely difficult. During the action enemy cavalry reached the division's rear, carried off the baggage and plundered the park, and on the retreat the division lost all its 12- and 8-pounders, overturned crossing ditches.
claims.rationale: Movement and means as the sources report them; no supply return was inspected. The late start followed the late delivery of Ney's orders (claim side-a-support), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'Dupont's division had set out from Albeck toward Ulm on 11 October at 11 a.m.'; Baraguey d'Hilliers, 'the troops are somewhat dispersed and will arrive rather late at their cantonments; they have marched or bivouacked all night in frightful weather; the roads are broken up and the artillery will have great difficulty in arriving'; 'a 4-pounder is under repair on 11 October'; 'our artillery, too inferior to the enemy's, was partly dismounted; several pieces had their horses killed; the snow and the rain, which had prevailed for several days, having made the ground extremely difficult, this inferiority was felt still more'; 'during the action the enemy cavalry moved onto the rear, carried off the baggage and plundered the objects of the park'; Krauss, 'where, coming upon the train of Dupont's division, it caused great confusion'; 'on the retreat the division lost all the twelve- and eight-pounders, which overturned in crossing ditches and could not be righted again'.

claims.value: Krauss says all side B's troops, even those that had not been under fire, had already suffered heavily. FML Rouvroy, the army's artillery chief, reported on 11 October that the wretched state of the horses made the artillery reserve unfit to operate, almost unfit for any movement; Krauss calls such states the result of the marches back and forth and two insignificant actions, and cites Mack's statement at his trial that the army's disorder and fatigue allowed no movement at all in those days. Despite this, Mack threw the troops in the position at Ulm into complete confusion, breaking up corps, division and even brigade formations without cause, and the greatest disorder reigned at Ulm.
claims.rationale: Condition as Krauss gives it from the Kriegsarchiv files; no supply return was inspected. The exhaustion came from the army's earlier marches and the disorder from Mack's arrangements before the action; Mack directed the army in fact, but Bodart names Schwarzenberg as side B's commander at Haslach (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. The trial's dates are in the OCR and are not restated. October permitted no movement at all'; 'despite this state of the troops Mack threw them into complete confusion in the position at Ulm. claims.value: Ney's letter to Dupont on the morning of the 11th said the enemy was struck by a terror with few examples and was retreating by Biberach to escape into the upper Tyrol, so the Archduke had probably left only a weak garrison in Ulm. On the march Dupont learned that the enemy held Thalfingen on his left, and his patrols met Austrian patrols toward Dornstadt; before entering Haslach he learned that a very numerous Austrian force was showing on the heights north of Ulm. Alombert and Colin say the enemy showed very superior forces and suggest that Dupont was perhaps counting on the reinforcement of 4,500 dragoons on foot with 10 guns and hoped the enemy had no more than 10,000 to 12,000 men. His journal says captured Austrian officers later stated that the whole army had bivouacked on the Michelsberg. Krauss says Dupont reported the concentration of the Austrian army at Ulm on none of the days before or after the action and seems to have realised only from captured officers' statements that he had had the whole Austrian army before him; Dupont's later letter claiming he learned on taking position at Albeck that the enemy army held the Michelsberg was, by Krauss, written long after the action.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge in the French official history, Dupont's journal and letters, and Krauss. Alombert and Colin's 4,500 and 10,000 to 12,000, read from the page image, are their conjecture about what Dupont expected ('peut-être'), not a report. Dupont's reports of 10 October on the enemy are in claim french-figures-for-side-b. English renderings (ours): 'is struck by a terror of which there are few examples: he is withdrawing by Biberach to be able to escape by the upper Tyrol'; 'it is therefore probable that Archduke Ferdinand will have left only a weak garrison in Ulm'; 'on the morning of the 11th a third instruction was sent to General Dupont'; 'during the march General Dupont learns that the enemy occupied Thalfingen on his left'; 'the reconnaissances on the right had likewise met Austrian patrols toward Dornstadt'; 'finally, before entering Haslach, Dupont learned that a very numerous Austrian troop was showing on the heights north of Ulm'; 'the enemy showed very superior forces, and the Marshal had prescribed not to risk an engagement in these conditions; but perhaps General Dupont was counting on the reinforcement of 4,500 dragoons on foot with 10 guns, and hoped that the enemy had no more than 10,000 to 12,000 men'; 'Austrian officers, prisoners of war, have since stated that their order of battle had been taken the day before and that the whole army had bivouacked on the hill of Saint-Michel'; Krauss, 'Dupont, however, remarkably reported the fact that the Austrian army was concentrated at Ulm neither on the 9th nor on the 10th and 11th, nor even on the 12th'; 'in short, it appears as if Dupont had become clear only through the statements of captured officers that he had had the whole Austrian army before him at Ulm'; Dupont, 'I learn at once that the enemy army, except its detached corps, occupies the Michelsberg before us, near Ulm'; Krauss, 'this error shows that the letter, whose date is not given, was in any case written long after the action'.

claims.value: Krauss says Mack would not believe he would be attacked at Ulm: it was raining and snowing, the enemy was sitting quietly in his quarters, and the Austrians would do the same. Austrian headquarters already knew that only part of Ney's corps had appeared at Günzburg. Mack's relation reported the attack as made by the French army of observation under Ney, and the Archduke wrote the next day that the Austrians had gained an advantage over one division of the enemy. Dupont later wrote that the enemy took his division for the advance guard of the French army following it.

claims.value: Krauss says Mack resolved on 10 October to march the army to Heidenheim that day, changed his mind in the night and decided to stay at Ulm, wishing to send FML Werneck's corps toward Stuttgart and on to Strasbourg. In the action, Krauss says, Mack contented himself with fending off the enemy. Mack's relation announced that the next day the army would advance down the Danube against the French army of observation and actively pursue its victory. Alombert and Colin say the enemy did not use his forces to make his success decisive, and that Dupont's resistance cost him a day and decided him not to continue his movement toward Nördlingen.
claims.rationale: Side B's plans as Krauss reconstructs them from the Kriegsarchiv files and as the French official history judges them; no passage read shows a plan for the action itself. Whether Mack's plans were those of side B's commander at Haslach is the responsibility question (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'on 10 October Mack resolved to march off to Heidenheim that same day'; 'Mack seems during the work, that is in the night to 11 October, to have changed his resolve and decided to stay at Ulm with the army'; 'he wanted to stay at Ulm, where he was in Abraham's bosom, and to send FML Werneck with his corps to Stuttgart and further as far as Strasbourg'; 'the planlessness of Mack, who contented himself with fending off the enemy'; Mack, 'tomorrow already we will advance down the Danube against this enemy army of observation and actively pursue our victory'; 'but he did not know how to use the forces at his disposal to make his success decisive'; 'Dupont's resistance made him lose a day, and decided him not to continue his movement toward Nördlingen'.

claims.value: In side A's accounts side B attacked. Dupont's division, ordered to surround Ulm, could not carry out the order and had only time to prepare for battle at Haslach: the enemy decided its movement on the spot, its artillery playing on the front of the French position while several infantry columns preceded by many squadrons came on against the French right and it deployed out of its entrenchments on the French left. Alombert and Colin say the division had been established at Haslach only a short time, its posts just placed, when the enemy attacked, and Dupont's later letter has the Archduke detach a large corps to attack him. The French bayonet charges and the fight for Jungingen, on which the French right rested, were made against these attacks.
claims.rationale: Coded from Dupont's division journal (read from the page image), his later letter and the French official history: side B took the offensive and Dupont accepted battle at Haslach; his charges were counterattacks from his position, which by the brief's rule do not make side A the attacker. Dupont's orders were to invest Ulm, but these accounts say he could not begin to carry them out. The accounts show side B's attack decided on the field ('décidé sur-le-champ'; the Archduke in Dupont's letter), so the posture is tagged commander_created; who in side B's command decided it is disputed (claim side-b-decisions). Krauss's account, coded separately, has the French attack first (claim posture-krauss). The Jungingen passage is from Titeux's account drawn from Dupont's manuscript memoirs, which Alombert and Colin quote in a note. English renderings (ours): 'the general had orders to surround Ulm, resting his right on the Blau'; 'he cannot carry out this order, he has only time to prepare for battle'; 'the enemy's movement is decided on the spot; while his artillery plays on the front of our position, he carries several columns of infantry preceded by a great number of squadrons against our right. He also deploys out of his entrenchments on our left'; 'the division had been established at Haslach only a short time, its posts had just been placed, when the enemy attacked'; 'as soon as the Archduke sees that our movement has been halted at the sight of his order of battle, he detaches from his position a large corps of infantry and cavalry to attack us'; '[Jungingen,] on which our right rests, and whose possession is indispensable to us'.

Dupont's division drove in the Austrian outposts at Haslach, threw back the battalions of the regiment Riese sent to support them and continued its attack against the Austrian right wing as far as Böfingen; after the fight on the southern wing had begun, Austrian troops were sent forward via Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right, and Dupont decided to forestall that attack. Krauss calls the action the attack of Dupont's division, and quotes Mack's report that the French attacked the army's right wing with great violence while Mack led a considerable part of the left wing into the rear of the enemy right.
claims.rationale: Coded from Krauss's narrative and the Austrian report he quotes: main attacks by each side on different parts of the field, so both_attacked. Dupont's attack followed Ney's order to invest Ulm, which Krauss calls clear but impracticable, and the passages show Dupont deciding to forestall the Austrian attack; the Austrian envelopment was decided on the field, by Schwarzenberg according to the Archduke and by Mack according to Mack's relation (claim side-b-decisions). Both attacks were decided at this engagement, so the posture is tagged commander_created. Krauss also says Mack contented himself with fending off the enemy (claim side-b-objectives), and the French accounts are coded separately (claim posture-french-accounts). The hour in the OCR is not restated. English renderings (ours): 'the division came upon the enemy outposts at Haslach, which were driven back'; 'these, however, were thrown back by the French, who now continued their attack against the Austrian right wing as far as Böfingen'; 'at the time when the fight on the southern wing had already begun, Austrian troops were directed forward over Jungingen, apparently to envelop the French right wing'; 'decided to forestall this attack'; 'under these circumstances the attack of Dupont's division took place on 11 October at ... in the afternoon'; Mack, 'that the army was attacked at midday on the 11th before Ulm by the French army of observation under Ney on its right wing with great violence'; '"our right wing repulsed all attacks with great steadfastness, while the quartermaster general FML Mack had a considerable part of our left wing advance and led it into the rear of the enemy right'.

open_questions: Deferred: the 1806 inquiry into Baraguey d'Hilliers' conduct and his justificatory memoir, whose papers Alombert and Colin print; the artillery commander's and Sahuc's reports beyond the passages they quote; Dupont's letters to General Sanson (Alombert and Colin, p. 523) and his manuscript memoirs (known through Titeux); Ney's report to Berthier of 12 October; Schönhals, Der Krieg 1805, and the relations of Mack, Gottesheim and Archduke Ferdinand, read only through Alombert and Colin and Krauss; Krauss's map (Beilage 26). Figures seen only in the OCR and not read from the page images are not recorded: the prisoners and guns in the artillery report (p. 51), the strengths and prisoners in Dupont's letter to the comte D. (pp. 512-513), the strengths and detachments of the dragoons on foot (pp. 38 and 45), and the hours in Alombert and Colin's narrative and in Krauss.

Most consequential gap: side B's engaged strength and loss. Krauss's 18,000-20,000 infantry and 2,000-3,000 horse is an estimate without a stated basis, and side B's loss is known only as the wounded brought into Ulm by 12 October and an unstated number of prisoners. The Austrian relations in the Kriegsarchiv (Mack's, Gottesheim's) or Schönhals, which Alombert and Colin call the best Austrian relation, could close it.

When Dupont first gave the 25,000: Alombert and Colin say he wrote it to Ney the same evening and print the passage in the 6th corps journal for 19 vendémiaire (11 October); Krauss says the first surviving document with the figure is the letter to Sanson dated 13 October, the day of the combat report to Ney (the report Alombert and Colin say was sent on the 21st, that is 21 vendémiaire, 13 October), and that Ney's report of 12 October gives no Austrian strength. The passages read do not say when the corps journal was compiled. Not resolved. The two printings of the evening letter also differ in one word: 'décisives' in Alombert and Colin's narrative (p. 54), 'dévouées' in the corps journal (p. 516), both read from the page images.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the result, Bodart's Austrian victory against Dupont's reports of a complete French victory, with both histories rejecting or qualifying his claim; Bodart's 25,000 for side B against Krauss's estimate of 18,000-20,000 infantry and 2,000-3,000 horse engaged and the French 20,000-25,000; Bodart's 6,000 for side A against the returns' 6,194 infantry and cavalry (our sum), Alombert and Colin's 6,400 and Krauss's 5,150 and 1,050; Bodart's 900 prisoners against Alombert and Colin's and Mack's 800-900 and Sahuc's 73 dragoons; Bodart's 11 guns and 17 wagons (Schönhals) against Mack's 11 guns and 20 wagons, Alombert and Colin's material list (9 guns and 31 caissons and carts, our sums) and Krauss's 5 guns and 23 wagons taken; Bodart's 43 officers against the 33 identified (our sum); side B's loss, Bodart's 1,100 against Dupont's 2,000 killed or wounded and 4,000 prisoners (7,000 in Krauss's account of his claims), the bulletin's 1,500 prisoners and Krauss's 1,100 wounded; and posture and fortification coded differently from the French accounts and from Krauss.
